{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+models+of+self-correction+and+error+detection+in+cognitive+architectures&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"From Artificial to Embodied and Physical Intelligence in Smart Manufacturing.\", \"abstract\": \"Manufacturing is evolving from automation-centered production toward systems capable of sensing, adaptation, and autonomous response across digital, mechanical, and material domains. Although recent progress has been largely driven by artificial intelligence, current manufacturing intelligence often remains external to physical systems and suffers from limited robustness, interpretability, and transferability in complex industrial environments. Here, we present a unified perspective on smart manufacturing through the framework of artificial intelligence (AI), embodied intelligence (EI), and physical intelligence (PI). AI provides abstraction, prediction, and generative capability; EI enables closed-loop perception, decision-making, and physical interaction; and PI embeds adaptive intelligence directly into materials, structures, and physicochemical processes. We further discuss how generative intelligence is beginning to connect these domains through inverse design, adaptive fabrication, and physics-constrained behavior realization. Recent advances in collaborative robotics, embodied digital twins, self-optimizing production systems, and physically intelligent materials, including self-actuating, self-healing, multistable, and shape-morphing systems, are reviewed. Finally, we propose an integrated AI-EI-PI framework spanning the full manufacturing lifecycle, highlighting a transition toward manufacturing systems in which intelligence is increasingly co-designed across algorithms, embodied agents, and matter itself.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.78384\", \"pmid\": \"42932218\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13703982\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.78384\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\":…

40 years of cognitive architectures: core cognitive abilities
and practical applications
Iuliia Kotseruba 1 · John K. Tsotsos 1
Published online: 28 July 2018
© The Author(s) 2018
Abstract
In this paper we present a broad overview of the last 40 years of research on cognitive
architectures. To date, the number of existing architectures has reached several hundred, but
most of the existing surveys do not reﬂect this growth and instead focus on a handful of
well-established architectures. In this survey we aim to provide a more inclusive and high-
level overview of the research on cognitive architectures. Our ﬁnal set of 84 architectures
includes 49 that are still actively developed, and borrow from a diverse set of disciplines,
spanning areas from psychoanalysis to neuroscience. To keep the length of this paper within
reasonable limits we discuss only the core cognitive abilities, such as perception, attention
mechanisms, action selection, memory, learning, reasoning and metareasoning. In order to
assess the breadth of practical applications of cognitive architectures we present information
on over 900 practical projects implemented using the cognitive architectures in our list. We
use various visualization techniques to highlight the overall trends in the development of
the ﬁeld. In addition to summarizing the current state-of-the-art in the cognitive architecture
research, this survey describes a variety of methods and ideas that have been tried and their
relative success in modeling human cognitive abilities, as well as which aspects of cognitive
behavior need more research with respect to their mechanistic counterparts and thus can
further inform how cognitive science might progress.
Keywords Survey · Cognitive architectures · Perception · Attention · Cognitive abilities ·
